children.heading: See it work
children.text: Three real research problems, each taken from question to cited answer: a word study that decided a translation, a query no concordance can ask, and the artistry of the text made visible.

children.heading: The engine
children.text: The database the demos run on, the research app built around it, and the ladder of guarantees that makes its answers worth trusting.

children.heading: The road ahead
children.text: Where this is heading, the four contributions that would move it faster, and how it stays free for the people it is for.

children.heading: Working together
children.text: Interoperability with the rest of the Bible translation movement is the point of the design, not an afterthought. This is also where to put your name if you want to follow the work or help test it.

children.heading: Quality control
children.text: What stands between a raw manuscript and an answer you can rely on: the six stages every text passes through, what each check actually proves, and the five holes that are not closed yet.

children.label: Every text moves through one pipeline

children.text: A database of the ancient world's literature, and a research app built on it, so that anyone translating the Bible can study a passage as if they were an attentive member of the original audience.

Every morning I put on a bracelet of black, orange, and red beads. It was made in Brazil by Indigenous translators working on an oral Bible translation with a mission project there. It is my reminder to pray for them.
They speak high-school to college-level Portuguese. For study resources they have a few translation helps in Portuguese, and for everything else, they ask ChatGPT.

I have spent fifteen years studying the Bible with the best desktop software available, and about ten of those studying the original languages with it. Since 2020 I have worked as an exegete, researcher, and team leader for the Spoken English Bible, an oral translation. Since 2023 I have been pioneering methods for studying emotions in Scripture to guide oral translators, and I published my thesis on that work in 2025.

The bracelet asks me a question I have never been able to shake: my brothers and sisters translating the Bible around the world deserve better than a chatbot's guesses. What would it take to put world-class exegetical evidence in their hands, in a language they read well, presented the way they communicate?

children.heading: You already know the tools fall short

children.text: If you work anywhere near Bible translation, you have felt it. In my experience, the concise resources translation teams rely on answer roughly 60% of the questions a real team asks. The other 40% gets filled by the translator's own assumptions, because there was nothing else within reach to consult.

The knowledge to answer those questions exists. But assembling it takes a specialist months, working in English, behind expensive licenses. I began my career in SIL doing exactly this kind of research, so I know what it costs. Some of that research changed how key passages were translated. More of it is still sitting in folders, unfinished, because the hours ran out. The shortfall is not for lack of sources. In a July 2026 survey of the 616 resources the largest open platform offers for a single chapter, ancient sources were cited by name throughout and quoted exactly once.

Two panels compared. On the left, a translator consults two dictionaries, then scatters across many disconnected databases, and the notes fade to dashed outlines beside an empty result. On the right, the same notes flow along drawn paths into one collated corpus and land as a filled result card carrying both a lexical and a cultural answer.

children.caption: Two dictionaries that were not written for this question, a dozen databases that do not talk to each other, and a schedule that runs out first.

Uniform metadata, lemmas and morphology on the originals, and search that takes a plain-language question. The translator does their own research, and not only the lexical kind: the cultural question becomes a query too.

children.text: Recent AI breakthroughs clearly ought to help. The open question is what, specifically, they should be aimed at, and my answer has three parts. The first is the picture above. Here are the other two.

children.heading: Write the brief, then read the sources

children.text: The second change is what happens once a question is well posed. You write a detailed research brief, the way you would for a research assistant who is good but needs telling. An agent collects the evidence across the corpus, organises it, and writes a synthesis at whatever length you asked for.

Then you read all of the sources yourself and come to your own conclusions, especially on the decisions that matter. That order is the whole design. The machine does the gathering, which is the part that used to eat the week. The reading and the judgment stay with the person who has to defend the result.

This is not hypothetical. One key-term study run exactly this way went from roughly five to twenty hours of specialist work down to about one, and its evidence changed a real translation decision across a whole New Testament. See It Work tells that story in full.

Two panels compared. On the left, a long stack of dashed note outlines accumulates with no report at the end of it. On the right, a brief at the top sends drawn paths into a small set of gathered sources, which pass a gate and compile into two filled report cards.

children.caption: Five to twenty hours of collecting before the thinking can start, and often the hours run out before it does.
About an hour to organised, cited evidence, with every source still in front of you to read and to disagree with.

children.text: Normally the poetry of the original is invisible to a translation team. You can read in a commentary that it is there. You cannot see it, and you certainly cannot see where it is.

The artistry analysis puts it on the text. The sound play in the Lord’s Prayer, the shape of a parallel series, each finding graded against ordinary contemporaneous language so that a pattern counts only when chance cannot explain it. See It Work runs that analysis live on Matthew 6, with the real detector output.

Then the part that matters most for a team working through a language of wider communication: comparable examples of what the biblical language is doing, rendered in the language the team is actually using. Not a note saying a pun is present, but a demonstration of what that kind of pun does, in words they think in.

Two panels compared. On the left, a block of text sits beside a dashed note that merely asserts artistry is present, with nothing marked on the text. On the right, the same lines carry marked spans, each joined by a drawn path to a graded finding, and below them a filled card of comparable examples in the team’s own language.

children.caption: A sentence in a commentary. Nothing marked on the text, no way to judge how strong the pattern is, nothing a listening audience could be given.
The artistry located on the line, graded against ordinary Koine, and matched to comparable examples in the language the team is translating into.

children.heading: One word can make a world of difference

children.text: My oral translation team needed to decide how to translate martureo, commonly translated as "bear witness." We needed to know exactly how the word was used in legal settings and when it was used metaphorically, because "witness" has taken on an important spiritual meaning in contemporary American Christianity. Changing from the norm would require substantial evidence.

children.quote: What does μαρτυρέω actually do across its New Testament occurrences, and how does its sense shift with speaker, setting, and audience?

children.text: In Origo, that study started with one search with the AI research assistant.

children.caption: Interactive: a lemma search, exactly as the app renders it. Click a result to open the aligned reader.
The real reader: original text and English side by side, with the search hits flashed. This screenshot, like every screenshot in this essay, is the actual app as it runs today.

children.text: I ran this study for real, for the Spoken English Bible's key-terms work. From question to evidence to write-up took about an hour. Done by hand, the same study takes me 5 to 20 hours, and this one's conclusions changed a real translation decision. That is the promise in miniature: not different answers, but the same careful answers at a speed a translation schedule can afford.

children.heading: A question no concordance can ask

children.text: Now a harder one, straight from my own thesis on the emotions of Luke 24. At dawn the women come to the tomb to anoint Jesus's body. How that scene feels, and how we read the apostles who dismissed their report, turns on something the commentaries never settled: in that world, who was actually expected to prepare and anoint a body for burial? Was it women's work, or did men share it?

children.quote: Across the ancient world, who actually prepared and anointed a body for burial, and was that women's work or did men share it?

children.text: No concordance can ask that, because a concordance indexes words, not who does what to whom. Origo can, because every text in the database carries 100 to 300 lines of metadata: era, language, people, places, the actions and speech acts in a scene, and the social dynamics of every interaction, including who holds power, how close the parties are, and what is at stake. Even with only a fraction of the corpus yet tagged, that already adds up to a social map of 33,000 participants across 23,000 interactions, the kind of map that can surface every scene in the ancient world where a body is prepared for burial, and who performs it.

When I wrote that thesis, no resource I owned could answer the burial-role question, so I set it aside, and the emotional reading of the scene stayed a notch less certain than it should have been. This is exactly the gap Origo is built to close. A corpus like this, queried across the whole ancient world in an afternoon, would have saved me hours of searching and spared the passage a real blind spot. The specialist's judgment then gets spent where it belongs: on what the evidence means.

Oral translation lives or dies by sound. The biblical authors knew that too: they wrote with puns, rhymes, and runs of words that begin alike, artistry that carried meaning for listening audiences. But a translator cannot carry over what the resources never showed them.

children.quote: Where exactly in this passage is the artistry, and how confident can we be that it is craft rather than chance?

children.text: Origo's Artistry suite answers with evidence, not impressions. The Structure viewer scores parallelism and chiasm across five axes and names the rhetorical figure; the Soundscape viewer detects sound play in the Greek and grades every find against a 4.5-million-word background of ordinary contemporaneous Koine, so a pattern only counts when chance cannot explain it. On its benchmark passage in Matthew 6, the sound-play detector recovered every device biblical scholars had already catalogued by hand.

children.caption: The Structure viewer on Mark 1: an epistrophe, the same word landing at the end of clause after clause, scored at 10σ and colour-graded by strength, rarer than 1 in 100,000 against the Greek New Testament itself. A run like that is the author building emphasis on purpose, exactly the shaping an oral translator will want to carry over.

children.text: Here is the Lord's Prayer as the Soundscape viewer hears it: the Greek laid out line by line with its word and syllable counts, and the sound plays the detector found listed on the right. The three most significant are already lit; tap any finding to add or remove its colour.

children.caption: Interactive: real detector output for Matthew 6:9-13, with the app's own class colors. ὀφειλήματα / ὀφειλέταις is the pair English keeps as "debts / debtors."

children.text: An oral translator who can see the craft can decide what to do with it: echo the rhyme, keep the pun, restructure the parallelism in their language's own idiom. None of that is possible while the artistry stays invisible.

Everything you just saw runs on one foundation: a corpus of the ancient world's literature relevant to the Bible, gathered from openly licensed sources and license-tracked file by file. Hebrew Bible, Greek New Testament, Septuagint, Dead Sea Scrolls, the Jewish literature, the Greco-Roman authors, the ancient Near Eastern texts, ancient translations, and tens of thousands of everyday papyri and inscriptions, the closest thing we have to hearing ordinary people talk.

Each text moves through one pipeline: an interlinear with morphology and roots identified, a literal English translation aligned to the scholarly divisions, 100 to 300 lines of metadata, and a vector index for semantic search. The result is a corpus that people and AI agents can query with the same precision, and every answer traces back to a source line.

Around the database sits the research app: a tiled workspace where search, reading, artistry tools, reports, and notes live side by side. Notes are plain markdown files you keep and can open in any editor. AI is optional throughout, and it runs through whatever you choose, from free local models on your own machine to the lightest cloud tiers. Your own legally owned PDFs, commentaries, and articles can sit beside the corpus and be searched the same way.

children.caption: The tiled workspace, with a live lemma search running beside the research reports it feeds. Notes and the artistry tools are a tab away in the same panes, and every pane moves.
The commentaries portal: your own library, indexed locally, searched by a free local model. Nothing leaves your machine.

children.heading: What works today, and what remains

children.text: A pitch is easy to write in the future tense, so here is the present tense in two columns. Everything on the left you could use this week; every screenshot in this essay comes from it. Everything on the right is real work still to do, and it is what the road ahead is for.

children.label: Structured search
children.text: Precision search over the whole corpus: a word’s root, the era and region, the theme, the speech act, the social dynamics of a scene, and the emotion in it. Describe what you want in plain language and a local model fills the filters, or set them by hand.

children.label: The literary-analysis views
children.text: Structure, sound play, semantic domains, cohesion, rhythm, figuration, and component order. Each one scores its findings against a background rather than asserting them.

children.label: The aligned reader
children.text: Original language and English side by side, aligned to the scholarly divisions, with search hits carried through into the text.

children.label: Workspace, reports, and notes
children.text: A tiled workspace where search, reading, artistry, research reports, and notes sit in movable panes. Notes are plain markdown files you own and can open in any editor. Your own legally owned PDFs sit beside the corpus and are searched the same way, by a local model, without leaving your machine.

children.label: The AI research coach
children.text: A plain-language question becomes a precise research brief, runs against the corpus, and comes back cited, with every tool call listed beside the answer and grounded citations visually separated from the model’s own inference.

children.label: Translations
children.text: About 3,150 texts are still in the queue for an English translation, 1,317 of them Greco-Roman literary works. Below the confidence gate a text is marked untranslated rather than guessed, which is the right behaviour and also why the queue is long.

children.label: Theme tags
children.text: Roughly 37,000 low-value documentary texts carry template summaries rather than real theme tags. They are indexed and findable; they are not yet richly described, and the tagging cannot start until the translation does.

children.label: Modern English
children.text: Much of the freely licensed English in the corpus is free precisely because it is nineteenth-century, and it reads like it. Everything in that class needs a modern-English revision.

children.label: The reference layer
children.text: Dictionaries, grammars, and background commentaries built on the corpus and verified by scholars. Designed in detail, and not begun.

children.label: The rest of the tools
children.text: Twenty-one tools and views run today, which is under half of the analytical methods the design calls for. The remaining ones are specified rather than speculative, and they cost time rather than money.

children.label: Honest statistics
children.text: The rarity numbers the artistry tools display are being rebuilt. The current scale conflates how long a pattern is with how artful it is, and applies no correction for how many places were searched. Where a baseline is provisional the interface says so on screen, and this correction is at the top of the queue, ahead of any new viewer.

children.heading: Built for how people actually learn

children.text: The knowledge layer rests on two models that have already proved themselves. Luhmann’s Zettelkasten is a networked slip-box: notes are small, atomic, and linked to each other, and the links are where the thinking accumulates. Leonardo’s notebooks are the other kind, observational and undisciplined, a place to put what you noticed before you know what it is for. Origo makes room for both, and keeps them distinct, because they are good at different things.

In practice that means a question captured by voice on a walk can become linked, cited research at the desk that evening, saved as notes tagged to the verses and topics they touch, so the next study session starts where the last one ended. The files stay plain markdown on your own machine. The interface decisions underneath this are not guesses either: they come out of my own research on cognition, learning, and memory, and out of five years of refining this workflow for my own study before any of it became software.

children.heading: Why you can trust what it returns

children.text: "AI" and "trustworthy" rarely sit comfortably in one sentence, so Origo is built as a ladder of guarantees. First, normal scholarly discipline: the corpus is built from identified editions with per-file provenance. Second, full traceability: every claim an AI assistant makes carries a citation chip that opens the source, and inference is visibly separated from evidence. Third, benchmarking: outputs are checked against resources translators already trust before they are recommended. Fourth, human review before anything is published for others.

The same discipline applies below the surface. Machine translations enter the corpus only above a 95% confidence threshold, and that number is not a figure the model invents about itself: it is scored against defined criteria. For a documentary text, for instance, the core elements of the transaction, who the parties are and what changed hands, must both be fully present and none may be lost, and a high self-assessment is overridden when the criteria contradict it. That is a stricter bar than we ask of most human translators. Below the line, a text is marked untranslated rather than guessed. Rarity claims in the artistry tools name their reference class and are corrected for multiple testing, and where a baseline is still provisional, the interface says so on screen. Above the individual checks sits a five-layer validator that runs on every change, and the corpus currently stands at zero schema or parse errors across all 80,036 files.

children.caption: The coach's evidence panel: every tool call and citation is listed beside the conversation, and grounded citations are visually distinct from the model's own inference.

children.text: That is the discipline in principle. Here is how it actually runs, as a text moves from a raw manuscript into the corpus. Click any step to see what happens there, which kind of model does the work, and where a human has to sign off.

children.label: How a text earns its place in the corpus
Identified sources
children.text: Every text is built from a named, published edition, and each file carries its own license and provenance. Nothing enters the corpus anonymously, so any claim can be traced back to a source a scholar already recognises. This is ordinary academic discipline, done before any AI touches the text.

children.label: Translation, by the strongest model
children.text: When a text has no usable English translation, the hardest judgment step, it goes to the strongest available frontier model, which translates it and returns a structured self-assessment of its own confidence. The heavy reasoning is deliberately given to the most capable model, not the cheapest, because this is where errors would do the most damage.

children.label: The 95% gate
children.text: A gate then routes that result against defined criteria, not a number the model invents about itself. A translation clears only if its confidence is at or above 95 and a rubric of the text's core elements confirms it; a high self-score is overridden when the rubric contradicts it. Below the line the text is marked untranslated rather than guessed. The empirical basis is real: on one hard book, the model cleared none of the texts without the rubric and almost all of them with it.

children.label: Tagging, kept in its lane
children.text: Only a cleared English translation is handed to a fast local open model for summary and theme tagging. That model works from the English alone; it never reads the raw Greek, Latin, or Hebrew. A model is only trusted with a task it can actually judge, so the languages it cannot read are never left to its guesses.

children.label: Deterministic validation
children.text: Every enriched text then runs a deterministic gate: schema checks, a controlled vocabulary, and a fidelity audit. This step has no model in it at all. It is plain, repeatable code, and it is the final automated arbiter before anything is allowed to commit.

children.label: A human signs off
children.text: Nothing commits automatically. Findings land in a review queue, and a qualified person has to approve them before any resource is published for someone else to rely on. The system is fast because the machine does the gathering; it is trustworthy because a human still owns the judgment.

children.heading: Every check, and what it does not reach

children.text: That is the ladder in principle, and the walk-through above is how a single text climbs it. This is the whole apparatus at once: six stages, and every named check over them with its own boundary written next to it.

A diagram is a persuasive object, and a green box labelled “quality control” drawn over a check that is sampled, warn-only, or unwritten will be believed. So each component below carries its state, and the known holes are named on the page rather than filtered off it. Click any component to read what its check proves and where it stops.

children.label: Verified
children.text: Built, and covered by a named check you could run yourself.

children.label: Partial
children.text: Built, but the check over it is sampled, warn-only, or incomplete.

children.label: Gap
children.text: A known hole. No check reaches it, and the entry names the fix.

children.label: Planned
children.text: Specced, with nothing running yet. Nothing on this map is in this state: everything here is either running or a named hole.

children.label: Acquire
children.text: Getting a text into the corpus from a named, published edition, with its license and provenance attached to the file.

children.label: Divide
children.text: Right-sizing a text into retrievable parts along the scholarly divisions rather than arbitrary character counts.

children.label: Translate
children.text: Making the text readable in English, or refusing to, which is the more important half.

children.label: Tag
children.text: Adding the metadata layers: themes, entities, speech acts, the social world, the metaphors.

children.label: Lemmatise
children.text: Word-level linguistics: roots and morphology, decided by a vote across independent sources.

children.label: Retrieve and report
children.text: What actually reaches a reader, and whether it earned the right to.

children.label: Layer 0: does it parse?
children.text: Proves the file parses. It says nothing at all about whether the content is right, which is the honest limit of every structural check.

children.label: Layer 1: does it match its schema?
children.text: Only as strong as that file class’s schema. A class with a permissive schema is checked in name only.

children.label: The permissive-schema trap, found and closed
children.text: Closed on 31 July 2026: that class is properly checked now, and a misspelled key is an error rather than a shrug. The shape of the bug is structural though, so a future file class added without its own branch could fail the same silent way, and no error count would reveal it.

children.label: Five works are stored twice
children.text: Both copies are individually valid files, so no file-level check can possibly see it. Closing it needs a duplicate check at the level of the whole manifest, because only a whole-corpus view catches this class of error.

children.label: Four collection names are really two
children.text: The vocabulary check confirms that a value is registered, not that two registered spellings mean the same thing. The fix is to normalise 23 straggler files and then add the merged pair to the check so it cannot recur.

children.label: The catalogue does not agree with itself
children.text: The catalogue’s header total and the table beneath it come from the same script and are never checked against each other. Found while building this map. The fix is an assertion that fails the build when the two diverge.

children.label: Layer 3: is the file well structured?
children.text: Warn only. A structural defect is reported and the commit proceeds anyway, which is a deliberate trade and still a weakness.

children.label: The 95 gate
children.text: Documentary and Jewish-source classes only. Greco-Roman literary translations pass through no equivalent gate yet, which is the largest single hole in the translation stage.

children.label: The same gate, enforced in the data
children.text: Catches a mislabelled file. It cannot judge whether the English is actually faithful; no automated check can.

children.label: The honest-failure bucket
children.text: A judgment about legibility, not about meaning. A perfectly legible text can still be misread.

children.label: The Jewish layer is translating, and clearing
children.text: One holdout sits at 94 on a single unattested word and is flagged rather than bluffed. That is the gate working, not the gate failing.

children.label: Most of the corpus has no translation yet
children.text: The gate is built and self-tested, and so far it has had almost nothing to gate. Tens of thousands of documentary texts carry no English at all: about 3,150 sit in the active queue as worth translating, and the remainder are receipts, lists, and labels carrying template summaries. The translation run itself has not started, because it has a real cost attached.

children.label: Layer 2: controlled vocabulary
children.text: Some of these warn rather than block, so a value can slip through and be corrected later.

children.label: Every quote must actually exist
children.text: Proves the quote is really in the text it is attributed to. It does not judge whether the quote was worth citing, or whether the claim around it reads it correctly.

children.label: The social-world layer check
children.text: Structural and vocabulary only. Whether the tagged social act is the right reading of the passage is not checked by any code, and could not be.

children.label: The metaphor layer check
children.text: The same boundary: it confirms the tag is well formed and grounded in the text, not that the metaphor is really there.

children.label: Registry cross-check
children.text: It reports rather than blocks, so a finding only matters if a person reads the report. Wiring it as a gate is the obvious improvement.

children.label: Layer 4: does the AI summary match the text?
children.text: Sampled per tranche, never corpus-wide. It has run over the inscription layers and a small Second-Temple sample and found no hallucinations, at a default of 30 files per class. Most AI-written summaries in the corpus have never been checked individually.

children.label: A passed audit leaves no artifact behind
children.text: For a project whose first value is traceability, this is the one check whose own result is not traceable: the graded manifests are gitignored, so the evidence lives in a log rather than a record. The fix is to commit them, or to write each tranche’s sample size and defect rate into a durable file.

children.label: A consensus vote, not a single tool
children.text: Where the sources disagree, or where only one source covers a token, accuracy falls back to that single source, and the vote cannot rescue it.

children.label: Accuracy by stratum, stated honestly
children.text: The 99% target is met on the New Testament only. Literary morphology at that level needs a trained tagger and is deliberately deferred rather than quietly assumed.

children.label: A report cannot ship unless it does its job
children.text: Checks that claims are cited, not that each citation supports the claim it is attached to. Quote grounding is a separate check, upstream of this one.

children.label: Pre-registered recall gates
children.text: One passage and five reader personas, measured against a hand-written expectation list. It cannot catch a gap nobody thought to pre-register, which is the category of gap that matters most.

children.label: The end-to-end judgment is a human read
children.text: Whether a finished report is actually good is judged by a person, so unlike the other checks it does not run on every change.

Twenty-four components across the six stages: fifteen verified, four partial, and five gaps. Those counts come from an evidence ledger that names the script, gate, or document behind every single one, and the ledger is the load-bearing part. The canvas is trustworthy exactly as far as its ledger goes and no further.

Publishing the holes is not modesty, it is the argument. A quality-control diagram that shows only what passes is marketing; one that names what it cannot reach is something you can check. All five are listed above in their stages, and every one of them names its fix.

Fast answers are the floor, not the ceiling. The goal is for experts to use this system to produce open-access dictionaries, grammars, and commentaries: drafted with AI assistance over the corpus, verified by qualified scholars, and free to translate into any language of wider communication. A pilot on Mark 1 has already produced drafts I would set beside the commercial resources I own, and every step of that work is being saved as a reusable workflow so the next drafts start better. The pipeline is also content-type agnostic, and the designed second corpus is church history and the theologians, from the biblical era into the twentieth century.

children.label: Semantic roles
children.text: Tag the semantic role of every sentence component in the original languages, following the best-tested cross-linguistic classification. This unlocks corpus studies precise enough to ground lexicography.

children.label: Speech-act scripts
children.text: Group tagged speech acts into higher-order scripts, like the admission, regret, and request that together make an apology, so translators can compare whole social moves across cultures.

children.label: Metaphors and frames
children.text: Tag conceptual metaphors and semantic frames, first testing what scholarship has proposed, then extending it, so meaning above the word level becomes searchable.

children.label: Dictionaries
children.text: Original-language dictionaries with two or three senses per word, explaining further nuance through the metaphors and frames a sense participates in, instead of sense-lists twenty entries deep.

children.label: Editions in more languages
children.text: The same resources built in and translated into major languages of wider communication, not English only.

children.label: Speech to speech
children.text: A translator listens to a passage, thinks aloud, and the assistant engages their questions with cited evidence, by voice, in their language.

children.label: Specialized models (a hypothesis)
children.text: Stated as a hypothesis, not a capability: models a fraction of frontier size, fine-tuned and continued-pretrained on this corpus, should approach frontier reasoning inside this one domain, because a general model spends its scale being expert in everything at once. The test is defined before the claim is: benchmarked against gold-standard corpus tasks, and nothing is offered as a capability until it clears them.
At my current capacity this is months of focused building, not weeks. The sequence above matters more than any date: each layer is built and checked before the next one leans on it.

Here is where the road leads. A study session happens out loud: the translator talks, the system answers from the corpus, and the exchange is saved as notes tagged to the Bible verses it touched. Those notes belong to the team rather than to one laptop.

So a consultant arriving at a translation decision can see the exegetical trail behind it: the conversations, the study notes, the evidence that was actually in front of the team when they chose. Above that sits what the AI holds for the whole project, the team’s language sketch, their anthropology sketch, their translation skopos, their workflow, and their standard resources.

With those loaded it can do things generic advice cannot. It can compare this language’s typology against another’s and say which solutions have tended to work for that shape. It can spot where the receptor culture and the biblical cultures do not line up. And it can surface the deep-culture blind spots a mother-tongue translator is least likely to see coming, which is precisely the kind of gap an outside consultant used to be the only way to find.

Some of this is running already, and it is worth being exact about which part. The coaching layer is in beta today: a working coach that loads a real language sketch, an anthropological sketch, a translator profile, and a team brief carrying the team’s methodology, exegesis standard, skopos, and key-terms policy, and that answers with citations you can resolve. Study sessions are running too: a dictated reading comes back as cited engagement and is filed as verse-anchored notes. The shared team database and the voice-to-voice loop are designed and in progress, not built.

Two panels compared. On the left, one person’s notes sit in a single dashed file that goes nowhere, and the reasoning behind a decision is absent from the result. On the right, three people’s sessions flow along drawn paths into a shared store keyed to verses, and from there into a filled decision card that still carries its trail, with the loaded sketches shown feeding the same store.

children.caption: Study notes in a personal file. By the next revision the reasoning behind a decision is gone, and the next consultant starts from the text alone.
Verse-tagged notes from every session, shared across the team, with the exegetical trail still attached to the decision it produced.

children.heading: Four ways to move it faster

children.text: Everything above is running today on one practitioner’s time and a consumer subscription’s worth of AI. Four kinds of contribution would change its pace, and the first three are what I would ask for first.

children.label: Beta testers
children.text: Translation teams, consultants, and scholars willing to use it while it is still rough, and to say plainly what works and what breaks. This is the need I would fill first: the design questions that matter most are the ones real use exposes and no amount of planning finds. You can put your name down on the Working Together tab.

children.label: Funding to finish the foundation
children.text: The automated steps, translation, tagging, and indexing, are throttled by AI capacity rather than by design. Funding converts directly into corpus layers finished sooner, and the foundation is close enough now that finishing it is a matter of months rather than years.

children.label: Contributors building owned resources
children.text: The resources this field most needs cannot be licensed openly, so they have to be built: commentaries, a Creative Commons Greek dictionary, and Greek and Hebrew grammars. Drafted with the corpus, verified by qualified scholars, and then free to translate into any language of wider communication.

children.label: Experts in the design loop
children.text: Lexicographers, discourse linguists, and translation consultants to keep pressure-testing how the metadata layers are defined while they can still change. Once a layer hardens, its assumptions are expensive to revisit.

children.heading: Free for Bible translation, licensable beyond it

children.text: My commitment is simple: for people doing Bible translation, these services stay free. That is who the bracelet is for.

But the same engine answers questions far beyond translation, and the wider world already pays well for far less capable tools. The system is being designed so it could be licensed outside the Bible translation movement, to academic, publishing, and general biblical-studies markets, with proceeds funding further development and the wider work of SIL around the world. The sources themselves are openly licensed and license-tracked per file, and commercial terms would be cleared per collection before any such offering.

There is reason to think that lane is real rather than wishful. In every serious field, verified knowledge sustains paid subscriptions, because a wrong answer costs the reader more than the subscription does. Corpus products hold paid markets of their own that are decades old: the Thesaurus Linguae Graecae and the Loeb Classical Library have both been licensed to institutions for a generation, on far less analytical power than this. And keeping it free for Bible translation is not charity bolted onto a business. It matches how philanthropy in this ecosystem already flows, toward the translation work itself, which means revenue from the wider world is what lets the translation lane stay free without anyone being asked to fund it twice.

Origo is not trying to replace anyone's translation software. It is augmentation, not competition: an exegetical foundation that other products in the Bible translation movement can build on, draw from, and hand their users.

That commitment is structural, not sentimental. Texts and notes are plain markdown. Licenses travel with every file. The AI layer is optional and provider-agnostic, down to free local models. Resources produced from the corpus are creative-commons by design. And the roadmap's resource layers are being shaped so shared libraries and translation tools across the movement can consume them directly.
If you build tools for Bible translation, my chief desire is that Origo makes your product better. I would rather adapt to your standards than invent competing ones.

children.heading: Two ways to be part of it

children.text: The bracelet I described at the start is why I would rather build this with translators than for them. If you want to follow the work, or to put it under real pressure, both start with an email address.

children.label: Progress updates
children.text: Every month or two I write what actually moved: which corpus layers finished, what the tools can do that they could not last time, and what broke. No marketing, and no one else gets your address.

children.label: Beta testing
children.text: I am not going to pretend there is a polished product waiting for you. The foundation is close, and when there is something worth an hour of a translator's time I would rather hand it to people who will say plainly what breaks. Tell me what you work on and I will come to you when your part of it is ready.

children.label: I would like to be a beta tester
Language, project, or role. A line is plenty.

Joshua Frost is an oral Bible translation exegete, researcher, and team leader with SIL International. He has served the Spoken English Bible since 2020, published his thesis on emotion exegesis for oral translation in 2025, and has spent his career developing methods translators use to study Scripture so they can bring it to life in their languages.

Both projects live in a private repository while the engine is still being built; access is available on request. Every screenshot in this essay is the app as it runs today, and both interactive demos replay unedited output from the live engine.
